video_title: 🟢 LIVE: The CLARITY Act's Make-or-Break Moment
gist: A crypto-policy panel (DeFi Education Fund's Amanda Tuminelli, Solana Policy Institute's Miller, and TRON/Digital Sovereignty Alliance's Adrian Wall) dissects the first combined CLARITY Act draft just 14 days before a Congressional recess, concluding the ethics provision is the key blocker to passage, that Polymarket odds of 2026 passage have fallen from over 80% to 37%, and that failure to pass before recess likely kills the bill for the rest of the decade.

themes.theme: This week's combined CLARITY Act draft

insights.claim: The draft released this week was the first time the Senate Banking Committee and Senate Agriculture Committee halves of the CLARITY Act were combined into a single unified bill text.
insights.speaker: Amanda Tuminelli, DeFi Education Fund
insights.so_what: Marks the first point at which the industry and lawmakers can evaluate the bill's full scope together rather than piecemeal, a key procedural milestone ahead of a possible floor vote.
insights.quote: the draft that we saw this week was the first combined draft of the clarity act that we saw.

insights.claim: The DeFi-specific provisions in the new combined draft, including the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act protecting developers who don't custody user funds from money-transmitter liability, are unchanged from earlier drafts, which the DeFi Education Fund views as a positive sign since no new problems were introduced.
insights.speaker: Amanda Tuminelli, DeFi Education Fund
insights.so_what: Signals that developer-protection language, viewed as the most important part of the bill for decentralized infrastructure builders, has survived negotiations intact so far.
insights.quote: it maintains the blockchain regulatory certainty act, which in our view is the most important part of this legislation for software developers building decentralized infrastructure.

insights.claim: The two major new additions in this week's draft are a Title 9 law-enforcement section (which won a same-day endorsement from the Fraternal Order of Police) and a new ethics provision required by Senate Democrats and reportedly agreed to by President Trump the prior week.
insights.speaker: Amanda Tuminelli, DeFi Education Fund
insights.so_what: The law-enforcement endorsement removes one prior objection to the bill, narrowing the remaining fight almost entirely down to the ethics provision.
insights.quote: the federal order or fraternal, excuse me, order of police uh just endorsed the legislation uh about an hour ago.

themes.theme: The ethics provision as the make-or-break sticking point

insights.claim: The ethics provision as currently drafted includes a sunset clause and only takes effect 360 days after the full CLARITY Act is signed, meaning if the bill passes in fall 2026 the provision would provide roughly only one year of effective conflict-of-interest protection before lapsing with no clarity on what follows.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Undercuts the political framing that the ethics clause is a serious, lasting reform, since its practical enforcement window is very short relative to the underlying conflict-of-interest concerns it's meant to address.
insights.quote: this ethics bill... only comes into effect 360 days after uh the entire clarity bill's passed... There's really only a year of effective protection of this ethics clause... and then it's done.

insights.claim: The current ethics provision does not extend conflict-of-interest restrictions to adult children of officials, which Adrian Wall says is defensible as a matter of legislative drafting difficulty (adult children are financially independent), but is one of several gaps making the provision unacceptable to Democrats.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Clarifies which specific ethics-provision gaps are negotiable design tradeoffs versus which (the sunset clause) are viewed as the real dealbreaker.

insights.claim: As of this panel, no Senate Democrat has signaled any openness to the ethics provision as currently written, and all three panelists agree it is the single biggest obstacle standing between the current draft and a bipartisan floor vote.
insights.speaker: Amanda Tuminelli, DeFi Education Fund
insights.so_what: Tells investors and industry watchers exactly which single provision to track for signs of a breakthrough or a stalled bill.
insights.quote: there's not been any hint at all that any Senate Democrat is okay with it.

themes.theme: Vote math and the legislative calendar crunch

insights.claim: Passing the CLARITY Act is generally described as needing 7-8 Democratic votes, but Adrian Wall argues the real number needed is higher because several Republicans (he names Tillis and both Senators Johnson, plus recalls a senator who voted no on the earlier GENIUS Act) cannot be assumed as guaranteed yes votes either.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Reframes the vote-counting narrative that's often simplified to '7-8 Democrats needed' as understating the true difficulty, since GOP defections could raise the effective threshold significantly.
insights.quote: I'm not so sure they have all the Republicans lined up for this either... If I'm in the Republican seat, it's more than seven that you need.

insights.claim: The bloc of roughly 12 Senate Democrats seen as the likely swing votes (including Gillibrand, Booker, Warner) is, per Adrian Wall's direct conversations on Capitol Hill, 'not close to yes' as of this taping.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: A direct, first-hand read of the actual vote count that is more pessimistic than the industry's public messaging, useful for calibrating passage-probability estimates.
insights.quote: of the 12 that there's this Democrat coalition of 12... they're not close to yes. I mean, I was on Capitol Hill this morning. I can tell you they're not close to yes.

insights.claim: Polymarket odds for the CLARITY Act being signed into law in 2026 have fallen from over 80% earlier in the year to 37% at the time of this panel, with odds dropping further after this week's draft release.
insights.speaker: host, The Defiant
insights.so_what: A real-money prediction market confirms the panel's qualitative pessimism, giving investors a quantified, trackable proxy for passage odds rather than relying solely on political rhetoric.
insights.quote: poly Target odds for clarity uh signed into law 2026 have been trending down... and it's now at um uh 37%... from you know over 80% earlier this year in February.

insights.claim: With Congress 14 days from recess, the practical floor-vote calendar is extremely tight: Monday is unavailable, Tuesday is consumed by Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral, leaving only Wednesday and Thursday of next week as viable floor days, after which the following week has a very short legislative session competing with other priorities before the August recess.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete, near-term calendar constraint investors can use to time their expectations for a possible vote, rather than treating the timeline as open-ended.
insights.quote: you've got Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral and you've got Wednesday and Thursday as an option. I don't see it happening next week for cloture.

insights.claim: Panelists agree that if the CLARITY Act does not pass before the upcoming August recess, the next realistic legislative window is roughly three weeks in September, but proximity to the midterm elections is expected to make bipartisan compromise there far harder, implying the bill likely would not pass again until sometime in the 2030s if it misses this window.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Frames the next two weeks as an existential, not just important, window for the bill — a binary near-term catalyst for any crypto-regulation-sensitive position.
insights.quote: if it doesn't pass out of the Senate in the next few weeks... the next realistic chance we'll have is... certainly will be sometime in the 2030s.

themes.theme: Is CLARITY passage secretly political theater?

insights.claim: Adrian Wall argues that Republicans, Democrats, traditional financial institutions, and even Coinbase may not actually want the CLARITY Act to pass, describing the process as substantially political theater rather than good-faith bipartisan negotiation.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: A sharply against-consensus read that should temper industry optimism that all major stakeholders are genuinely racing to pass the bill.
insights.quote: Republicans don't want to pass clarity. Democrats don't want to pass clarity. Financial institutions don't want to pass clarity. Coinbase doesn't want to pass clarity. There, I said it.

insights.claim: Adrian Wall's theory is that some Republicans may deliberately let a CLARITY Act floor vote fail so they can blame Democrats heading into the midterms while continuing to collect campaign donations from both the crypto industry and traditional finance PACs.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Suggests the bill's political value to some lawmakers as a fundraising and messaging tool may exceed its value as actual policy, a dynamic that could keep the bill stalled indefinitely regardless of technical negotiation progress.
insights.quote: we'll pretend this is the WWE and we'll make a big song and dance... we'll be able to say, 'Look, industry, we're your champion and it's all the Dem's fault.'

insights.claim: Adrian Wall points to Coinbase's unwillingness to compromise on governance and conflict-of-interest language (specifically rules against trading against customers) despite active Capitol Hill lobbying, as evidence the exchange may not be negotiating in good faith toward a bipartisan bill.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Names a specific, checkable behavior (lack of movement on customer-conflict governance language) that investors can watch as a signal of whether major industry players are genuinely pushing for passage.
insights.quote: they have not given an inch as far as I understand on any of the compromise on some of the governance language... trading against their customers.

themes.theme: What CLARITY actually does for token classification

insights.claim: The bill designates all tokens as commodities by default but layers a securities-style disclosure regime (audited financials, use-of-proceeds, management team disclosures) onto tokens classified as 'ancillary assets' — those raised via fundraising to build something — making it, according to Miller, the most disclosure-heavy digital asset bill proposed to date, more so than the Digital Commodity Exchange Act or the DCCPA.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Gives crypto issuers a concrete compliance roadmap (heavy disclosure but a clear legal path) rather than the current binary risk of being deemed an unregistered security.
insights.quote: it is by far the most disclosure heavy bill we've ever seen that's inclusive of Dem-led bills like the digital commodity act and the DCCPA.

insights.claim: Tokens like Bitcoin fall into a separate 'network token' category that can exit disclosure obligations entirely by passing a two-part test: first a decentralization/lack-of-control test, then an efforts test showing the original fundraiser is no longer engaged in more than nominal ongoing entrepreneurial or managerial activity.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Establishes a clear, testable legal mechanism for a token to 'graduate' out of securities-like treatment as a project decentralizes — a template investors can apply to assess any given token's current regulatory status.
insights.quote: if you pass that test, you can move on to the second test, a efforts test... you'll be subject to these disclosure obligations [if not].

insights.claim: The bill explicitly protects developers performing only technical infrastructure roles — running a validator, operating a node, creating an oracle service, or simply providing a user interface — from securities and commodities exchange act registration requirements.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Removes a major legal overhang for infrastructure-layer crypto participants (validators, oracle networks, front-end developers) who have long faced ambiguity about registration obligations.
insights.quote: running a validator, operating a node, creating an oracle service, um simply providing a user interface... those things are not the type of activity that those statutes are meant to regulate.

themes.theme: Remaining gaps: legacy tokens and RWAs punted to regulators

insights.claim: Adrian Wall identifies a gap in the bill's transition/liability-shield language: tokens from projects that matured from a centralized founding team into a DAO (or whose founding team's managerial efforts have long ceased) may lack the governance structure needed to complete the network-token certification process within the bill's transition-rule timeframe, exposing secondary-market holders to ongoing legal ambiguity.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, technical drafting gap that could leave a meaningful subset of mature, decentralized tokens in continued legal limbo even after the bill passes.
insights.quote: tokens which were previously traded in a secondary market they may require... assistance of a third party for the network token certification process and that may require more time than that's provided in the transition rule.

insights.claim: Adrian Wall is pushing to add a 'clean slate' fix modeled directly on the 2022 LIBOR Act, which automatically converted all LIBOR-referencing contracts to SOFR to avoid mass litigation; his proposed CLARITY Act analog would automatically shield secondary-market token holders and participants from liability when a token's original team no longer exists to complete re-registration.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete legislative precedent and fix for a real transition-period risk, worth tracking to see if it gets incorporated into the final bill text.
insights.quote: Congress stepped in and said... anything that was LIBOR is now automatically SOFR. No more of this litigation... coming back to this token text for me, I'm calling this clean slate.

insights.claim: For tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) like tokenized equities and bonds, the CLARITY Act largely punts to regulators — for example, Section 505 directs the SEC to clarify how on-chain securities markets and secondary trading of tokenized securities should operate, rather than settling the framework in statute.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Tells RWA-focused crypto investors not to expect the bill to resolve tokenized-securities rules directly; the real outcome will depend on subsequent SEC rulemaking regardless of whether CLARITY passes.
insights.quote: it directs the SEC to clarify how onchain securities markets should operate... it uh on RWA days is broadly a punt to the regulators to figure it out.

insights.claim: Even without CLARITY Act passage, the SEC and CFTC are already working on RWA/tokenized-securities rulemaking out of deference to Congress, but any such agency rules would lack durability and could be reversed relatively quickly by a future administration with different policy priorities starting in 2029, unlike statutory law.
insights.speaker: Miller, Solana Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Explains why statutory passage still matters even for provisions the agencies could implement unilaterally — durability across administrations is the real prize, not just the substance of the rule.
insights.quote: the issue is durability... to the extent there's an administration with a dramatically different policy in 2029... they could just revoke those rulemakings.

insights.claim: Panelists warn that failure to pass CLARITY would create prolonged regulatory uncertainty that is 'kryptonite' to long-term crypto investment planning, making US crypto ventures effectively uninvestable at institutional/venture scale and pushing serious development offshore to jurisdictions like Singapore and the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: A direct capital-flow warning: absent statutory clarity, expect crypto innovation capital to migrate to friendlier foreign jurisdictions, a trend investors in US-based crypto startups should weigh.
insights.quote: without this regulatory clarity it's just... not possible [to invest]... you're going to see a huge... crypto ice age.

insights.claim: Adrian Wall predicts that without CLARITY, US crypto discourse will remain narrowly confined to stablecoins and dollar dominance for the next five years, since the broader wave of innovative applications being built by developers who 'haven't been heard from yet' won't be able to launch domestically.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Sets a specific, checkable five-year forecast — if US crypto innovation narrows mainly to stablecoin narratives with little else emerging, that's consistent with this failure scenario playing out.
insights.quote: we'll be talking about US dollar dominance and stable coins now for the next five years and that'll be it.

insights.claim: Companies have been operating on the assumption of a friendlier US regulatory environment (e.g., activating token fee switches, treating tokens as non-securities); failure to pass CLARITY could force some of that behavior to reverse back toward the more defensive posture common during the prior 'Gensler era' enforcement approach.
insights.speaker: host / Adrian Wall
insights.so_what: Highlights a real, near-term operational risk for crypto businesses that have already begun acting on the assumption of a more permissive regime.

insights.claim: Panelists agree that even without CLARITY passing, the SEC under the current administration is not expected to return to Gensler-era enforcement aggressiveness against crypto projects, but this could change dramatically if a less crypto-friendly administration (they cite a hypothetical Elizabeth Warren presidency in 2028) takes power.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Frames the near-term enforcement risk as low but the multi-year political risk as high, reinforcing why locking in statutory (not just administrative) protection matters for long-horizon investors.
insights.quote: if Elizabeth Warren, for example, was the presidency in 2028, then... everyone's going to jail.

insights.claim: Beyond the well-known bloc of 12 swing Senate Democrats, Adrian Wall flags the American Gaming Association, tribal gaming associations, and a newer, gaining-momentum coalition of Democrats as underappreciated opposition forces working against CLARITY's passage.
insights.speaker: Adrian Wall, Digital Sovereignty Alliance / TRON
insights.so_what: Identifies additional, less-covered lobbying opposition that could further complicate passage beyond the widely discussed ethics-provision fight.
insights.quote: we didn't talk about today the American Gaming Association or the... tribal gaming association and that whole new coalition of Democrats that are rising up to challenge this.
